rationale: B wins by not mistaking volume for strategy. Its "The hard part of a circular sneaker is the mail" angle finds the operational story hiding inside the sustainability claim, which is a real editor assignment. A has the sharpest single headline with "On says its shoe subscription \"closes the loop\" - it won't say how big the loop is," but it pads the set with "does the rest of the running category have to follow?" - a trade-press maybe, not a story yet.
gaps_in_A: "On's circular-shoe expansion raises the question: does the rest of the running category have to follow?" overstates the competitive story. The update gives On growth and a rollout, not evidence that rivals must respond.
"Shoes join the rental economy" is a little sloppy. The facts say subscribers mail shoes back to be ground down and remade, not that shoes are rented and recirculated.
"moving a core product line to this model" is an overclaim. The source says Cyclon is a running shoe, not that it is a core product line.
A misses the clean reverse-logistics angle. It asks "what happens on non-return," but never turns the mail-back/remake system into its own supply-chain story.
gaps_in_B: B buries the strongest accountability angle. "Proof it needs: ... the recycling rate" appears inside other angles, but there should be a standalone green-claims story around the undisclosed recycling rate.
"take-back programs are widely seen as the operational graveyard of circular retail" may be true, but it is not in the supplied facts. As written, it smuggles in an unsourced premise.

"a major athletic brand is moving a core product from purchase to subscription nationwide" overstates the record. The update says Cyclon is a running shoe subscription, not that this specific shoe is a core product.
"Meet the runner who never owns their shoes" is too quickly refused as hallucinated. No named subscriber is supplied, but a customer-story angle is viable if On can produce a real early subscriber.
